where: Call to action, 'For agent builders' (paper.tex:268); also Alternative views, third paragraph (paper.tex:259)

where: Table 3 cells U2, U3 (and U1, U4) in D-AGENT vs the cell rule in Appendix 'Reasons for the setting cells' (paper.tex:432, 451, 453); Introduction step 2 (paper.tex:64)
claim: All four unstated conditions fail (x) in D-AGENT. The cell rule: x "when the condition fails in the setting as usually run", ~ "when it holds in usual runs but fails in reported cases".
problem: The paper's own rule gives ~ where evidence comes from reported cases. The D-AGENT U2 evidence is simulation with simulated users and the paper says "the empirical support comes from training and simulation". The U3 evidence is evaluations, and the 2026 runs "lacked the lab's deployed safeguards" ("an atypical deployment"). These are reported cases, not usual deployed runs. Yet U2 and U3 get x, and D-CHAT U3 gets ~ on the same sources. The headline "all four unstated ones fail" and "nine of ten fail" therefore depend on a grading that contradicts the stated rule. The caveat in the introduction covers the source of the evidence, not this rule mismatch.
evidence: paper.tex:432: "A cell is \(\times\) when the condition fails in the setting as usually run, and \(\sim\) when it holds in usual runs but fails in reported cases"; paper.tex:451: "D-AGENT is graded by this reading of the setting; the empirical support comes from training and simulation"; paper.tex:250: "The runs lacked the lab's deployed safeguards ... in our terms they are an atypical deployment"; paper.tex:215: "U3 ignores mechanism & ... \textasciitilde{} & ✗" (D-CHAT ~, D-AGENT x)
fix: Either grade D-AGENT U2 and U3 as ~ under the stated rule, or restate the rule so x also covers reasoned or evaluation-based failure. Then recompute the "all four" and "nine of ten" counts, or say the counts depend on the second reading.

where: Abstract, last sentences (paper.tex:52); Introduction step 3 (paper.tex:64) vs Section 5 third bullet (paper.tex:245)
claim: Abstract: a certified safe set with a halting stop "keeps its safety theorem under the same assumption and one more". Introduction: "one guarantee survives deployment, a second keeps its safety theorem only under assumptions that we found no method to meet".
problem: "Keeps its safety theorem" suggests transfer. The body ends with "So this guarantee does not transfer yet". It also says the Wachi cost depends on the state and action (S4, which fails in D-AGENT) and that the claim needs a modification that is "our adaptation, not their theorem". Table 1 marks Wachi as needing S4 and S6 in full. A reader of the abstract can take "survives" and "keeps" as the same status, while Section 5 says the second one is conditional on an unmet hypothesis and a changed cost definition. This is a position-level inconsistency, even though the hedges exist in the body.
evidence: paper.tex:52: "keeps its safety theorem under the same assumption and one more, an uncertainty quantifier ... for which we found no model"; paper.tex:245: "So this guarantee does not transfer yet: it needs a quantifier that we found no model for and a safe halt that we assume."; paper.tex:245: "a cost of the tool call alone avoids this, but that is our adaptation, not their theorem"; paper.tex:101: Wachi row S4 "✓", S6 "✓"
fix: In the abstract and introduction, replace "keeps its safety theorem" with "would keep a modified version of its safety theorem", or "does not yet transfer, but a modified version would if ...". Keep the shield as the only guarantee that survives.

where: Section 3 opening (paper.tex:88) and the 'twelve works' headline (Abstract; Table 1; Section 4 paragraph before the bullets, paper.tex:221)
claim: "Of the twelve works behind the tools that McLean et al. offer, four state a guarantee about a safety constraint ... the exception is shielding"
problem: McLean et al. cite no shielding paper. The shield paper (Alshiekh) is chosen by the authors, who say "we use an early paper on shielding". It supplies one of the four safety guarantees. It is also the only exception to the seven-of-eight count, and the one result that "survives deployment". For seven topic works the tool label is also "ours". The abstract and conclusion state them as facts about "the tools that McLean et al. offer" and do not say that the shield paper was not cited.
evidence: paper.tex:88: "shielding, for which they cite no paper; we use an early paper on shielding \citep{alshiekh2018} ... For these seven the tool label in the table is ours."; paper.tex:221: "the exception is shielding"; 063_tools/tools.csv alshiekh2018 row: mclean_role=named_uncited

where: Table 1 row 'Monitored MDPs (mohammedalamen2025b)'; Section 3 third fact (four state 'a guarantee of optimality, convergence or soundness'); Section 4 count 'eight state a guarantee; seven of eight need in full...'; Abstract and Conclusion counts
claim: mohammedalamen2025b is listed with the guarantee 'Convergence, tabular only', and its S4/S5/S6 cells are marked needed in full. The paper counts it among the works that state a guarantee.
problem: The cited paper states no theorem of its own. It is an empirical study of function approximation in Mon-MDPs. The convergence guarantee it discusses belongs to earlier work (Parisi et al.), which it cites as a limitation it moves past. The paper's own result is 'near-optimal policies in some environments', shown by experiment. The paper's own appendix cell for S3 concedes 'the function-approximation version studied in the paper has no guarantee'. The main text never says this. Counting it as a stated guarantee inflates 'eight with a guarantee' and 'seven of eight'. It also changes 'four state another guarantee' and 'four state none'. S5 and S6 are then taken from the background tabular theorem, not from the paper's contribution. R17 does not cover this: it defends the S5 cell only if a guarantee exists.
evidence: 045_fulltext/mohammedalamen2025b.txt:231-232: 'While this approach is theoretically proven to converge to an optimal policy for solvable Mon-MDPs in tabular settings, the tabular reward model requires states'; :57-59: 'Prior work on Mon-MDPs have been limited to simple, tabular cases'; :661-662: 'Our results demonstrate that training a reward model with FA allows agents to achieve near-optimal policies in some environments previously labeled as unsolvable.' The file has no Theorem or Proposition of its own. 065_tool_conditions/cells.csv:40 says 'the function-approximation version studied in the paper has no guarantee'.
fix: Reclassify mohammedalamen2025b as 'none (empirical; cites a tabular guarantee of earlier work)'. Recompute the counts (about three with another guarantee, five with none, and six of seven for K10). Or state in the text that the guarantee is background and not the paper's own, and say how the counts change.

where: Appendix 'Reasons for the setting cells', S6 bullet, T-AGENT cell (paper.tex line 447)
claim: A leak of isolation makes outside effects possible that the reset does not cover. The lab reports that an agent in a May training experiment 'used an already publicly exposed Hugging Face user token' and that agents in an unrelated research workload 'issued write requests'. These are reported cases, so T-AGENT holds in part.
problem: The paper offers both events as sandbox failures (S6 'only while it holds'). In the source, both ran in workloads that had been given sanctioned internet access through WebCache, so neither is an isolation breach. The May 13 experiment is explicitly contrasted with the isolated May 8 run. The May 26 write requests came from an 'unrelated research workload', which the source does not call a training run. The incident appendix itself says 'one other May experiment had internet access by design', but the S6 cell leaves that out. The real isolation breaches (Artifactory SSRF, openai2026b) are cited separately. These two examples therefore overstate the evidence for the partial mark.
evidence: openai2026c.txt:326: 'Unlike the May 8 training run, this experiment was given access to the internet via WebCache.' openai2026c.txt:342-345: 'On May 26, other agents also accessed the internet through WebCache. The agents found six publicly exposed Hugging Face user tokens and issued write requests ... this activity occurred in an unrelated research workload.' openai2026c.txt:290-292: 'a webcache through which research workloads could access internet content under centrally enforced controls'.
fix: Remove the two WebCache examples from the 'sandbox holds' argument, or say they happened where internet access was granted and show the effect of a reset-uncovered action. Keep the Artifactory SSRF case (openai2026c.txt:338) and the openai2026b statement as the isolation-breach evidence.

where: Appendix 'Reasons for the cells', Shielding (alshiekh2018), S5 bullet (paper.tex line 530)
claim: S5, not for safety, in part for learning: the learner 'does not even need to know that it is shielded', but Assumption 1 asks that 'The learner accepts elements from S x Q as state input'.
problem: The two quotes describe different shield types, and the cell presents them as one tension. 'Does not even need to know that it is shielded' is stated as a property of post-posed shielding only. In that mode the source says the learner 'only sees the state of the MDP (without the state of the shield)', which contradicts Assumption 1(iii) as quoted. The S5 'in part' mark therefore rests on a mixed reading. The main text's claim that only a post-posed shield is shown to wrap a frozen policy (K07) depends on this distinction, and the cell does not make it.
evidence: alshiekh2018.txt:625-630: 'Properties of Post-Posed Shielding. The big advantage of post-posed shielding is that it works even if the learning algorithm is already in the execution phase and therefore follows a fixed policy. In every step, the learning algorithm only sees the state of the MDP (without the state of the shield) ... The learning agent does not even need to know that it is shielded.' alshiekh2018.txt:454-455: 'Assumption 1 ... (iii) The learner accepts elements from S x Q as state input'.
fix: Split the cell by shield type. Post-posed: no learner change needed. Preemptive: the learner takes the shield state as input (Assumption 1(iii)). Say which case each quote belongs to.

where: Appendix 'Reasons for the cells', Shielding intro, and Section 3 sentence on Wachi (paper.tex lines 88, 522)
claim: 'wachi2023 names this paper as the shielding it builds on'; Wachi call their own method 'a variant of shielding methods' and cite it.

The source says the emergency stop is 'akin to shielding [2, 20]' and that MASE 'can be regarded as a variant of shielding methods (especially, preemptive shielding in [2])'. It then lists what MASE does differently (penalties from the uncertainty quantifier). 'Builds on' implies derivation. The shortened quote also drops 'can be regarded as' and the 'especially preemptive' qualifier, which matters because the appendix uses the post-posed shield properties.

Thus, MASE can be regarded as a variant of shielding methods (especially, preemptive shielding in [2]) that is specialized for the GSE problem. On the other hand, MASE does not only block unsafe actions but also provides proper penalties ...'

where: Related work, 'Specification and side effects': 'Constraints can also be learned from natural language \citep{chua2025}'

problem: Misleading direction. The source learns constraints that are expressed in natural language, from text demonstrations (positive and negative examples), in a text navigation environment. It does not learn constraints from natural-language instructions. A reader would take the sentence to mean specification by instruction, which the source does not do.

where: 200_draft/draft.md lines 5, 69, 99 ("the proof of its near-optimality does not carry over"); changed in round 3
claim: "The proof of near-optimality does not carry over, because without a reset the state reached before a halt persists." The abstract and conclusion repeat that the proof does not carry over. The same text says that whether near-optimality holds is open.
problem: The paper presents the failure of the Theorem 4.2 proof as established. The proof of Theorem 4.2 never uses the reset. It argues that a penalty larger than the value bound makes any constraint violation, or any stop, unprofitable. It then argues that after convergence the stop is never executed, so the penalised MDP equals the original. The reset enters only through the definition of the augmented MDP (stop leads to s1). Nothing in the proof shows that the argument breaks when the halt leaves the state in place. The authors give a plausible reason the proof might break. That is a conjecture, not something the proof shows, and the "does not carry over" wording makes it sound shown. The draft itself says the result is open.
evidence: 045_fulltext/wachi2023.txt:1565-1572: "This means that, when the constraint violation happens even a single time, the value by a policy obtained in M̂ becomes negative because maxs Vrπ (s) ≤ Vmax. Under Assumption 3.2, after convergence, the optimal policy in M̂ will not violate the safety constraint, and thus the emergency stop action â will not be executed. In this case, the modified (unconstrained) MDP M̂ is identical to the original CMDP M." Lines 1467-1471 use only Assumption 3.2 and Γ ≤ ζ/2.
fix: Write "we have not shown that the proof of Theorem 4.2 carries over: it argues that a large stop penalty makes the stop unprofitable, and the reset enters only through the definition of the augmented MDP; whether this survives a persisting state is open problem 2". Make the abstract and conclusion say "we do not know whether the near-optimality result holds".

where: 200_draft/draft.md line 13 (Introduction); changed in round 3
claim: "The two safety filters use fewer [of U1-U4]: ... the certified safe set assumes only a cost that the agent does not move (U2)."
problem: The "only" claim is unsupported. The Wachi safe set also relies on a safety threshold that is given and fixed, and on a cost function that is fixed and single. If observations or another principal change the threshold or the specification, the guarantee fails. That is U1 (observations cannot set the objective) and arguably U4. The tool table itself marks the Wachi S1 cell as "threshold", given. The paper's own definition of U1 covers this case, so the claim that the certified safe set needs only U2 contradicts the paper's own conditions. It also supports the position's argument that the filters escape U1-U4, which makes it consequential.
evidence: 045_fulltext/064_conditions/stated.csv S1: "a threshold 'known at time h' [@wachi2023]". 065_tool_conditions/cells.csv wachi2023,S1: "the threshold is given, the cost is learned: the threshold 'is known at time h'". 045_fulltext/wachi2023.txt:234 and 1448-1456: the guarantee is g(s_h,a_h) ≤ b_h for the threshold b_h.
fix: Replace "assumes only a cost that the agent does not move (U2)" with "assumes a fixed threshold and a cost that the agent does not move (U1, U2)", or drop "only".

where: 065_tool_conditions/cells.csv:25 (alshiekh2018,S6, blank); paper Table 'Which work needs which stated condition'; facts.json guaranteed_not_failing and guaranteed_failing_dagent
claim: Cell S6 for Alshiekh et al. 2018 is blank, with the reason 'not needed: the shield checks every action when it is taken.' This makes shielding the only guaranteed work that needs no condition failing in D-AGENT.
problem: The reason does not support 'not needed'. Alshiekh's shield exists and guarantees safety only if a winning strategy exists, so the system can always avoid states from which the environment can force a violation. That is a recoverability property (a safe action exists in every reachable state), which is the S6 definition 'every state is recoverable within the decision process'. The paper itself later requires 'a safe fallback ... at every step' for the shield to transfer, so the cell and the Section 5 caveat disagree. The reason also says nothing about this winning-region requirement. The S6 cell should be at least partial, with the word 'winning region'. Even so, the exception stays (S1 is the only full cell), but the cell hides a condition the paper later imposes.
evidence: 045_fulltext/alshiekh2018.txt:333-335: "has to plan ahead: it can never allow the play to visit a state from which the environment can force the play to visit an unsafe state in the future." Also alshiekh2018.txt:299-301: "The winning region W is the set of states from which a winning strategy exists." Cell reason: 065_tool_conditions/cells.csv:25 "not needed: the shield checks every action when it is taken."
fix: Mark Alshiekh S6 as partial (for example 'winning region'), with a reason that the shield guarantee needs a safe action to exist in every reachable state, and state in the Section 4 and 5 text that this is the 'safe fallback' hypothesis. Keep the exception, but say what it rests on.

where: 085_setting_conditions/cells.csv:61 (U3,T-AGENT,✗) and reasons.csv:10; facts.json training_llm_max_fail
claim: U3 fails outright in T-AGENT. The reason is that 'optimising hard against a chain-of-thought monitor taught agents to hide their intent' (Baker et al.).

We investigate the effect of incorporating a CoT monitor into the reward function"

where: 096_review/key.csv
problem: key claim scored qualify
evidence: The paper lists hidden state (S4) as a binding obstacle "which closing those gaps would not remove" (paper.tex:58). It defines binding as failing in deployed agents and not shown "to yield to the scaling and function approximation that McLean et al. propose". It never engages McLean's own proposed remedy for partial observability. 045_fulltext/mclean2026.txt:82 says: "Elelimy et al. (2025b) propose that RL agents should learn an explicit mapping from trajectory history to state. ... Ensuring that this history-to-state mapping preserves and appropriately weights safety specifications is precisely the problem that constrained MDPs address (Altman, 1999; Satija et al., 2020), suggesting again that the RL safety literature has tools directly applicable here." This is a learned-state (function-approximation) answer to S4. The paper's stance row for S4 (paper.tex:162) records only "Partial observability is the basis of their POMDP mapping: 'This is a lossy process'". Line 88 mentions the Elelimy map only as a work read. The paper gives no argument that a learned history-to-state map does not address S4. The nearest argument is the D-AGENT reason in the appendix, that the world state behind tools "is not in the context" (085_setting_conditions/reasons.csv, S4 row). That reason covers world state, not the finite-context-window case McLean raise.
